data.title: Arkona, Rethra and other pagan sanctuaries of the Western Slavs
data.excerpt: Among the Slavs, roofed pagan temples were built only in the lands along the Elbe and the Baltic, where they survived into the 12th century. German chroniclers left detailed accounts of them: Thietmar's Riedegost, Adam of Bremen's Rethra, and above all Arkona on Rujana, where the four-headed Svantovít was guarded by a retinue of 300 horsemen until the Danes destroyed the sanctuary in 1168.
data.metaTitle: Arkona and Rethra – pagan sanctuaries of the Western Slavs
data.metaDescription: Most Slavic sanctuaries stood under the open sky; true roofed temples such as Arkona on Rujana and Rethra arose only in the Elbe and Baltic regions.

keyFacts.label: Period
keyFacts.value: Pagan temples in the Elbe and Baltic lands still in the 12th century (in the territory of present-day Slovakia paganism ends in the 9th century)

timeline.title: Thietmar's death — the oldest report on Svarožič
timeline.description: The chronicler Thietmar of Merseburg, who gave the oldest and trustworthy report on the god Svarožič and the sanctuary of Riedegost, died in 1018.

timeline.title: The sacred horse of Rethra carried off
timeline.description: The sanctuary's prophetic horse, which stepped over spears, was carried off as booty, evidently in battle, by Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt.

timeline.title: The end of the sanctuary of Rethra
timeline.description: The text gives no exact year, only the range “at the end of the 11th or in the 12th century”.

timeline.title: The statue of Triglav in Szczecin hacked to pieces
timeline.description: Bishop Otto had the statue of Triglav hacked to pieces and the three silver heads sent to Rome.

timeline.title: Arkona overthrown by the Danes
timeline.description: The Danes, rivals of the Rani, overthrew Arkona; King Valdemar had the statue of Svantovít dishonoured, hacked to pieces and burnt, and the Slavs were forced to be baptised.

timeline.title: Schuchhardt searched for Svantovít's temple at Arkona
timeline.description: The German archaeologist discovered the remains of a square building which he took for the sanctuary he was looking for.

timeline.title: An attempt to locate Rethra at Feldberg
timeline.description: Schuchhardt attempted to identify Rethra with the Feldberg hillfort beside the lake of the same name.

timeline.title: Herrmann refuted the identification of Feldberg with Rethra
timeline.description: More recent excavations showed that the Feldberg sanctuary is of a different type and earlier (7th–8th century), and therefore not identical with Rethra.

timeline.title: Berlekamp's re-evaluation excavation at Arkona
timeline.description: It showed that Schuchhardt's “remains of the temple” were rather traces of the inner fortification; the sanctuary itself was evidently swallowed up by the sea.

timeline.title: The sanctuary at the Feldberg hillfort comes into being
timeline.description: The dating of the Feldberg sanctuary to an earlier period, the reason why it cannot be identified with the historical Rethra.

blocks.text:
Above the cliffs of Arkona an eagle's nest rises high

Where the beating waves strike the eastern towers
A valiant eagle sits upon a throne of rock-
Guardian of the Slavic lands, free son of the heavens

O Slavic eagle, protect the nations of the Slavs
Protect the Slavic customs and the Slavic tongue
Protect us and our native land
Keep watch from the morning, keep watch through the day
Patrol past midnight with the keenest sight.

children.text: The absolute majority of Slavic sanctuaries in the territory of present-day Slovakia stood under the open sky, as is confirmed for us by the sanctuary from
Most pri Bratislave

, which is described elsewhere. True pagan temples of the Slavs in the form in which we know them from the later Christian period — that is, roofed buildings — arose only in the Elbe and Baltic regions. Here we find pagan temples still in the 12th century, whereas in the territory of present-day Slovakia paganism was replaced by the new faith in a single God already in the course of the 9th century, above all as far as the larger centres of power are concerned. In the course of the 10th to 12th centuries the German inhabitants of the Baltic and Elbe lands took the struggle against paganism as a pretext for their war aims, and in this connection they left us numerous descriptions of the pagan gods and sanctuaries of the Slavs who lived there.

blocks.text:
Where the eastern seas make the cliffs of Arkona resound

And above the steep headland the eagle reigns
Where in a deep valley a settlement rests
Mirrored in the pale blue water

That most beautiful land is my Rujana
My best-beloved fatherland

children.text: RETHRA

The oldest mention comes from Thietmar, and it concerns Riedegost, the centre of the Redarian tribe. A wooden sanctuary stood here in the middle of a grove, on animal horns set in its foundations, which evidently served an apotropaic function — a similar practice has been established archaeologically, for example, in the foundations of the fortification at Gdańsk, where aurochs horns were found. The outer walls of the sanctuary were decorated with numerous carved images of gods and goddesses; inside the temple stood statues marked with the names of the gods, headed by the chief deity Svarožič, and beside them banners and war standards. According to Thietmar of Merseburg, who died in 1018 and gave the oldest and at the same time very trustworthy reports about this god, he was originally called Svarožič. Svarožič, son of the god Svarog, god of the sun and of fire, was venerated in the 11th and 12th centuries in Russia as well. In the 11th century the name Svarožič disappears from the sources on the Elbe Slavs and the same god is called Radegast or Radigast, after the original name of the sanctuary. Thietmar describes the sanctuary and the rites in great detail. In the land of the Redarians there is said to have stood a strong fort of three-sided form with three gates, called Riedegost, surrounded by a sacred wood in which trees were never felled. Two gates of this fort were accessible to all; the third, the smallest, on the eastern side, led to a path down to the lake. In the fort there was only one sanctuary, masterfully built of wood, which rested, as has already been said, on a foundation of the horns of wild animals. On the outside it was decorated with images of beautifully carved gods and goddesses.

children.text: Inside the sanctuary stood statues of the gods in helmets and mail, and each god had his name carved at the bottom. First among them was Svarožič (Zuarasici), especially venerated by all the pagans. There were also standards there, which were brought out only in time of war. All this was guarded by the priests, who alone had the right to sit when sacrifice was made to the gods or when they sought to appease them; the others present stood.

blocks.text:
Do you see the land where the gull flies
Above a beach bathed in sun?
Where in a cleft of rock the fearless eagle is enthroned.
He gazes into the distance, guarding his domain
Covered with flocks of sea birds
In hundreds of bays their voices can be heard

children.text: Again and again...

A later witness from the end of the 11th century — Adam of Bremen — knew this sanctuary under the name Rethra, while the god, whose golden statue was said to rest on a purple couch, he calls Redigast. The temple, four days' journey distant from Hamburg, stood at a place surrounded by a deep lake; a wooden bridge led across it, by which passed those who wished to sacrifice or to ask for prophecies from the oracle there. The prophecies were made by means of a sacred horse which stepped over spears in a particular way. In 1068 Bishop Burchard of Halberstadt carried this horse off as booty, evidently in a battle to which it had been led. Rethra itself, however, evidently came to an end later, at the end of the 11th or in the 12th century.

In 1922 the archaeologist C. Schuchhardt attempted to locate Rethra at the Feldberg hillfort on the shore of the lake of the same name. The more recent excavations of J. Herrmann in 1967, however, did not confirm this assumption; the Feldberg hillfort did indeed have a sanctuary, but of a different type, and moreover it dates from a much earlier time, from the 7th–8th century, so that it cannot be identical with the historical Rethra. The sanctuary there consisted of a simple rectangular building with an indication of an entrance space, separated from the hillfort by a symbolic ditch. Its presence in such an ancient hillfort suggests that sanctuaries of this kind arose in this area very early. At the time when Thietmar was writing his chronicle, the Elbe Slavs must already have had a larger number of temples, since according to his testimony every land had its sanctuary, even though not every one of them need have been a temple building in the true sense of the word.
ARKONA

blocks.alt: Arkona, Rethra and other pagan sanctuaries of the Western Slavs

children.text: The place of Svarožič — Radegast was taken by Svantovít, the god of the Rani from the sanctuary at Arkona on the island of Rujana (Rügen). Perhaps no Slavic god has had so many scholarly and semi-scholarly articles and studies written about him. Some researchers considered that he was in fact not a pagan god at all, but a pagan deification of St Vitus, to which the similarity of the name and some of the chroniclers' statements invited them. But whatever root Svantovít's name may have arisen from, it is certain that in the 12th century he had nothing whatever in common with the Christian saint and that he was a full-blooded pagan god with all the prerogatives, claims to power and attributes.

blocks.text:
From the depths of the sea, from the deepest bed
Eternal bells sound, muffled
They ring to spread the tidings of an enchanted city of old.
Sunk in the embrace of the tide
The ruins have stood firm.
They leave golden flashes
Glittering on the surface of the sea.

children.text: Svantovít rose in the 12th century to a leading place among the Baltic and Elbe Slavic gods above all thanks to the commercial, economic and military successes of Rujana and the Rani, and also because the other pagan gods were gradually falling away. Gifts were brought to him not only by pagans but also by Christian rulers, if they wished to be on good terms with the Rani. The dues paid to Svantovít and his priest were regular and were paid by local people and foreigners alike. A third of the enemy's armament and of the booty won in wars also belonged to him. Svantovít had not only a priest but also his own retinue, made up of 300 horsemen. These warriors handed over to the priest, for the god, all the booty and the profits of raids and wars. Svantovít's property was kept hidden in a chest under lock and bar and included money, ornaments, costly fabrics and other objects, for example a precious cup from the Danish king.

children.text: Svantovít's temple did not stand in an isolated place, but on a plateau in the middle of the town; it was, however, enclosed by a wooden palisade and had only one entrance. The enclosing fence itself was decorated with carving and painting, all of it said to be crude. Inside the enclosure was the outer temple building with a red roof. The inner temple structure was formed only of posts, between which hung fabric screens. In it stood an immense statue of superhuman size with four necks and four heads, two of which looked forward and two backward. Its hair was cut in the usual style of the inhabitants of Rujana, and the moustache likewise shaved. In its right hand it held a metal horn filled with wine. From the state of the wine, with which the priest filled the horn every year, the harvest of the coming year was foretold. The statue's garment reached to the shins, and the legs were carved, joints included, so masterfully that the join was visible only on careful observation. Near the statue lay a horse bit, a saddle and numerous divine insignia, among which a sword stood out above all, with the splendid chasing of its scabbard and hilt and its silver exterior. Only the priest was allowed to enter the sanctuary, whose treasures were guarded by the retinue of 300 horsemen already mentioned, and he had to do so holding his breath — for every intake of breath he had to go back to the entrance.

At Svantovít's sanctuary prophecies were also made and sacred rites performed. When the prophecy was unfavourable, a military campaign or trade negotiations were postponed to a more suitable time. The agricultural cult was of great importance. Every year the priest filled Svantovít's horn with fresh wine and after a year examined how much had gone. If there was wine enough, the harvest was to be good; if little, there would be a crop failure. Accordingly they then regulated the laying up of stores and the consumption of food in that year, so that it would last even in years of poor harvest. In honour of Svantovít and for the purposes of prophecy a round cake with honey was baked, almost as large as a man. After the rite a great festival and feasting followed, at which the offerings presented to the god were also consumed. Svantovít had his own white horse, which only the priest was allowed to ride; at night, it was said, the god himself rode it — then the horse was sweating and dirty. According to the chronicler Helmold a human being was said to be sacrificed to Svantovít every year, a Christian chosen by lot.

blocks.text:
And the sailor,

Who sees that magic flicker but once
In the dazzling evening glow
Will always return to that place
Though reefs threaten him all around.
Will always return to that place
Again and again...

children.text: In 1168 Arkona was overthrown by the military and commercial rivals of the Rani — the Danes. The Danish king Valdemar had the statue of Svantovít dishonoured, hacked to pieces and burnt before the eyes of the horrified and humbled Rani. He then forced the Slavs to be baptised.

In 1921 the German archaeologist C. Schuchhardt attempted to find Svantovít's temple. He discovered the remains of a square building in which he saw the sanctuary he was looking for, and a drawn reconstruction of it was then taken over by a number of publications. From the point of view of present-day research methods, however, the results of Schuchhardt's excavation cannot be regarded as reliable, and the re-evaluation excavation of H. Berlekamp in 1969–1970 indeed also showed that what Schuchhardt took for the remains of the temple were rather traces of the inner fortification of the hillfort, while the sanctuary itself evidently stood on a spot that the sea swallowed up long ago.

At a hillfort on Rujana surrounded by marshland and resorted to only in times of the danger of war, three further massive sanctuaries stood, splendidly decorated, roofed, with purple hangings instead of walls; the largest of them was surrounded by an enclosure. Rugievit, Porevit and Porenut were venerated in them.
You will find a large number of photographs and a short text from our expedition to Arkona in
this article
OTHER SANCTUARIES
According to Ebbo, admirably decorated sanctuaries to the value of 300 talents were built by the inhabitants of
Gochov

(Chozegow, today's Gutzkow); Herbord speaks of only one temple. They protected idols of extraordinary size and “unbelievable beauty”, which it was difficult to move, so that during Otto's missionary activity they had first to be cut down and only then dragged away to be burnt. The invisible demon who dwelt here fled at the singing of the faithful, who were carrying a cross, in the form of a swarm of flies.
Of the other Elbe and Pomeranian gods we should mention, for example, Rugievit in the town of
Korenica

, who had an oak idol with seven faces. In Szczecin they venerated Triglav, who likewise had a temple decorated with carvings and paintings, and further smaller sanctuaries. He was a mighty god, “summus deus”, who, like Svantovít and Radegast, had a sacred horse by whose means prophecies were made. After 1128 Bishop Otto had his statue hacked to pieces and the three silver heads sent to Rome. The overthrow of Triglav's sanctuaries in Szczecin was helped by the common people, who are said to have ceased to respect the god when they saw that he could not defend himself. The people's help, however, sprang rather from another source: from the oppression of the priests, the rich merchants and the nobility, who defended their power precisely in Triglav's name.

children.text: One of the most remarkable Slavic temple structures was discovered at the hillfort of
Gross Raden

on the shore of Lake Sternberg. In the open area of the south-eastern part of the peninsula stood a single-roomed hall (7 × 11 m) linked by a narrow path lined with stelae to a wooden road that passed through the hillfort. Its rectangular ground plan was slightly bowed on the shorter sides, which were fitted with entrances. The walls were formed by a double row of planks sunk into the ground and pointed at the top, of which the inner row was load-bearing and the outer decorative. In the round, or rather lozenge-shaped, pointed carved heads at the upper end there emerge for us the suggestion of male and female figures. The inner area of the temple was damaged by a later ditch, so that no traces have survived of the placing of any idol. The inventory, however, included 6 horse skulls, 2 iron spears, a wooden shield and bowls on small feet. Above the temple door a cattle skull was hung. The Gross Raden hillfort is an original local architecture which attests the old tradition of Slavic building and refutes any other influences (whether Celtic or Scandinavian).

children.text: The temple at
Wolgast

, dedicated to Gerovit-Jarovit, was not described in any detail. We know only that during Otto's preaching the crowd became enraged, and that one of the clerics saved himself from their anger by fleeing into the temple, where he seized the sacred shield and, under its protection, then passed unharmed through the astonished crowd.

children.text: The famous port town of
Wolin

had a temple called “continu”, surrounded by marsh and preserving a sacred spear sunk into a great post. Its Latin designation is probably derived from the Old Slavonic ka.t, to which correspond Czech kút, Russian kušča, Serbian Kuča and Bulgarian kasta (= dwelling). The monks accompanying Otto took them, evidently as a result of a misunderstanding, for the spears of Julius Caesar — the monk of Prüfening gives Julin as a variant name of the town as well. It is not out of the question that two temples stood here, as is suggested by the two churches built on the same site after the acceptance of Christianity and dedicated to St Wenceslas and St Adalbert. Triglav was venerated at Wolin as well. Here Bishop Otto of Bamberg managed to destroy only the sanctuary; the golden god was hidden by a priest in the countryside in a hollow tree, and the pagans continued to bring him offerings.
